title: Discussion Questions
text: Discussion Questions question 1 In the first chapter, Kimmerer compares the Potawatomi story of the Skywoman to the Christian story of Eve and points out how their relationships to the earth vary. What do these stories about the first woman in these different cultures tell about them and their attitude about women? What is the lesson they share about human’s relationship with nature? Compare and discuss. question 2 Kimmerer gives the example of Evon Peter, who claimed he was raised by a river. In the same vein, Kimmerer herself claims to be raised by strawberries. Which part of nature would you consider you were raised by, and why? Describe what role nature has played in your life and how it has affected the person you have become today. question 3 Kimmerer talks about the differing concepts of private property economy and a gift economy. In the former, a gift is just a gift and is free to be used or not by the recipient. In a gift economy, a gift is used to build relationships and must be rooted in reciprocity. She applies this to land ownership. What else can these concepts be applied to? Discuss gifts and their cultural implications in different cultures. question 4 Kimmerer started taking classes in her native language, Potawatomi. There are only nine speakers left who speak it fluently. What do you think can be done to revive these almost-lost languages? How much effort should the government put into reparations and revitalizing these lost languages? Discuss how the US government and the settler community (European immigrants in the Americas) can make reparations for the loss of culture and language for the Native Americans. question 5 Kimmerer’s daughter refused to stand up for the American Pledge of Allegiance in her school. What do you think this pledge denotes, and why do you think she was refusing to acknowledge this? Can we truly be global citizens if we put our own country first? question 6 Kimmerer shares different stories and legends of the Potawatomi with readers. Which one of these did you like the most, and why? In what way does this specific story resonate with your own life? question 7 The author explains the concept of Honorable Harvest, which dictates to take only what you need and use everything you take. How does this differ from the practices in our modern-day society? How would it be possible for us to practice honorable harvest today? question 8 Kimmerer points out that the settlers behave like they are planning to go back to their homeland even after several generations. She says that the best way for them to blend in is to be naturalized and become one with the land. How do you think white people in the US can do this? How does this advice work for the next wave of immigrants in the US from Asia, Africa, and South America? question 9 On one of her college field trips, Kimmerer raised the question of how or even whether they could give back to nature in return for her gifts. Her students arrived at a number of interesting answers. What is your opinion about this? question 10 The book is all about the interactions between humans and their environment. The author gives her own example of her special relationship with certain plants. Is there a plant in your environment with which you feel a special relationship? Which one is it, and why do you feel this way about it? If not, why? Would your life be enriched with such a special relationship with a plant? Discuss. question 11 Kimmerer claims that we are linked in a co-evolutionary circle. The better the plant product, the more people tend to spread its seeds and nurture the plants. The thriving of one is in the best interest of the other. The author defines this as love. How do you see this working in other relationships? Discuss. question 12 The Three Sisters of indigenous agriculture are corn, beans, and squash. These three plants together have fed generations of Native Americans throughout North and South America. The three are often planted together, and each enhances and supports the other plants. Can you think of other sacred plants that are intertwined with each other prevalent in other cultures? What is the value of such indigenous farming practices? question 13 Kimmerer talks about the importance of ceremonies to keep people grounded in their land and their community. Do you agree? What are the good and bad points of continuing age-old ceremonies? Should they be an important part of our lives? Kimmerer also recommends that the European colonizers should adopt ceremonies from their homelands and regenerate them to bond with the new lands. Would this work? Discuss. question 14 Kimmerer describes the childhood of her children and how she tried to raise them with proper regard and enjoyment for nature. However, her children experienced it in a way much different from her own, and she points out that is true for everyone. Do you think this applies to all other things? Do we all see things from a slightly different perspective than each other? Why, or why not? If yes, why should this be so? question 15 Kimmerer shares her experiences of teaching botany in unique ways, trying to get her students to understand the harmony of nature and to feel a connection to her gifts. She talks about her experiences in the Bible Belt and was thrilled to make a connection with the students. In what way do you think Christian students bond with the land in comparison to others? question 16 Kimmerer has written two books in recent years after she completed her Ph.D. These are Gathering Moss: A Natural and Cultural History of Mosses and Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge and the Teachings of Plants . Which one do you like better, and why? In what way are these two books similar and/or different from each other? question 17 Kimmerer is a Native American woman and a member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation. She is also a proponent of Traditional Ecological Knowledge. In what way do you think these factors color her work? Would her work be different if she did not have this background? Discuss. question 18 Kimmerer’s courses at the university include Land and Culture, Traditional Ecological Knowledge, Ethnobotany, Ecology of Mosses, Disturbance Ecology, and General Botany. How do you think she can teach the love of the land through these subjects? question 19 Kimmerer makes an effort to combine her scientific passion for plants, forests, and biology with her native Potawatomi heritage and knowledge. Why do you think she feels scientific and real understanding of the land are different? Do you think they are mutually exclusive? Discuss. question 20 Kimmerer grew up in a rural area where she interacted every day with plants in the garden, woods, or even the wetlands. This led to a deep and sustaining interest in the diverse biological world around her. How did this help her develop a relationship with nature? Do you think it is possible for everyone in the world to have this experience? Is this an entitled attitude? Discuss. question 21 The author has written two books: Gathering Moss: A Natural and Cultural History of Mosses , published in 2003, and Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge and the Teachings of Plants , published in 2013. Which of these two did you like the best, and why? question 22 Kimmerer received her bachelor’s and master’s degrees in botany. She also completed her Ph.D. in plant ecology and has an honorary M.Phil degree in Human Ecology. How have these studies helped her connect to nature in real life? In what ways has this education conflicted with the traditional knowledge of her people? question 23 The author’s grandfather, Asa Wall, was forcibly sent to the Carlisle Indian Industrial School and deliberately and systematically uprooted from his people and traditional way of life. How do you think these experiences have shaped the First Peoples’ psyche in the US and elsewhere? question 24 Kimmerer tries to recover her lost heritage by communicating more with her community’s elders and holders of knowledge and by learning the Potawatomi language. She also ensures that she attends certain ceremonial events and is an enrolled member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation. Do you think it is possible to turn back time for these victims of colonization? Why, or why not? What are the different ways in which countries can help the First Peoples’ cultures thrive? question 25 The author is a proponent of Traditional Ecological Knowledge, which was first described by Fikret Berkes of the University of Manitoba as “a cumulative body of knowledge handed down through generations by cultural transmission, about the relationship of living beings with one another and with their environment.” What is this concept called in modern scientific language? Do you think this is something all humans have, or is it just a feature of the Native American culture? Can you think of other cultures that have developed such a relationship with nature? question 26 Kimmerer is also involved in projects involving helping her native Potawatomi tribe, the general Native American population, as well as the wider diaspora of non-white peoples in the USA. This includes sponsoring the Undergraduate Mentoring in Environmental Biology project, which helps non-white students by pairing them with faculty members. What do you think is the impact of such programs on minorities? In what way do you think such programs improve society as a whole? question 27 The author’s first job was as a microbiologist in Bausch & Lomb. Later, she completed her Ph.D. and started teaching. Why do you think she chose to teach as a career? In what way would her experiences in these jobs be different from each other? question 28 Kimmerer is active in conservation and ecology projects. She has been involved with the Strategies for Ecology Education, Development and Sustainability project, Ecological Society of America Traditional Ecological Knowledge Section, and has even participated in a discussion at a United Nations meeting on ecology. What are the advantages of these programs? Why were these programs implemented? Why did the author choose to be a part of these programs? question 29 Kimmerer is the director of the Center for Native Peoples and the Environment , an initiative geared towards sharing of modern environmental science and traditional environmental knowledge. How does this help people in general? Can Native American traditional environmental knowledge help people in China, Nigeria, or India, or do these countries require different environmental perspectives? Why, or why not? question 30 Kimmerer’s first book, Gathering Moss: A Natural and Cultural History of Mosses, received the John Burroughs Medal Award. Her second book, Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge and the Teachings of Plants , is the recipient of the 2014 Sigurd F. Olson Nature Writing Award. What is the value of such awards for books? What other awards would you nominate Kimmerer for? question 31 A special hardcover edition of Braiding Sweetgrass was published with a new introduction from Robin Wall Kimmerer in honor of the fortieth anniversary of Milkweed Editions. The book was reissued as an object of meaning that will last for a long time. Why do you think the publishing company chose this book for its anniversary reissue? question 32 Despite its success, Braiding Sweetgrass did not have a large-scale marketing campaign. Instead, it became popular through “word of mouth” and recommendations from one reader to the other. Why do you think some books do not require a large marketing campaign and still become a huge hit? What is it about Braiding Sweetgrass that it became a success? question 33 The few criticisms of the book state that the stories run together and are often repetitive, and the author’s presentation of the subject is completely one-sided, not taking into account the social problems of indigenous or traditional societies. What is your major criticism of Braiding Sweetgrass ? How could the book have been improved? Explain and discuss. question 34 The cover is designed by Tony Drehfal and contains an engraving as well as a deckled edge and a bookmark ribbon. The new edition also contains five colorful illustrations by artist Nate Christopherson. In what way does the cover complement the subject matter of Braiding Sweetgrass ? Is it important to have a cover that represents the content of the book? Discuss. question 35 Braiding Sweetgrass won the 2014 Sigurd F. Olson Nature Writing Award, given in honor of the literary legacy of Sigurd F. Olson to the best environmental writings in adult nonfiction and children’s literature. Why do you think it merited this award? question 36 The name, Braiding Sweetgrass , is a metaphor referring to the fact that the stories told in the book are made up of three strands: the traditional indigenous perspective about the environment, scientific knowledge about plants, and the beauty of the knowledge that plants themselves hold and can teach those who want to learn. If you were to suggest an alternative name for this book, what would it be and why do you think it would be suitable? question 37 Kimmerer has written two books so far: Gathering Moss: A Natural and Cultural History of Mosses and Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge and the Teachings of Plants . What should be the topic of her next book, if you were to choose for her, and why? question 38 Kimmerer talks about the bounty of strawberries and how she could call herself “raised by strawberries.” If you were to have a plant that could have raised you, which one would it be? Why do you think so? question 39 Kimmerer desires to connect back to her roots. A trained botanist, she desires to combine her scientific knowledge with traditional knowledge. She had also begun to take Potawatomi classes, of which there were only nine fluent speakers left at the time, and became a member of the Potawatomi Nation. If you were in her place, what measures would you take to reconnect with your lost heritage? Why do you think these steps would help you? question 40 A member of the Potawatomi Nation, Kimmerer is a botany professor and tries to mingle the two worldviews, scientific and traditional ecological knowledge, for a better understanding of plants. If Kimmerer were not a Native American, how do you think her relationship with plants would be, and why? Would it be similar or different? Why? question 41 Kimmerer grew up in a rural area where she interacted every day with plants in the garden, woods, or even the wetlands. This led to a deep and sustained interest in the diverse biological world around her. She thought of plants as companions and assigned them real-life roles that help people along. How do you think this book would have been different if she had been brought up in a city? question 42 Kimmerer’s family was a part of the exodus of Native Americans from their homelands to less fertile lands. Her grandfather, Asa Wall, was forcibly sent to the Carlisle Indian Industrial School and deliberately and systematically uprooted from his people and traditional way of life. In what way would the world be different if colonization had not happened? How would native Europeans relate to other cultures in this context? question 43 The cover for Braiding Sweetgrass is designed by Tony Drehfal and contains an engraving as well as a deckled edge and a bookmark ribbon. If you were to design a cover for this book, how would you do it, and why? question 44 Despite its success, Braiding Sweetgrass did not have a large-scale marketing campaign. Instead, it became popular through “word of mouth” and recommendations from one reader to the other. Do you think the result might have been different if the book had a large-scale marketing campaign? How well do you think this book would have been received in that case? question 45 Braiding Sweetgrass has a rating of 4.58 on Goodreads and 4.8 on Amazon. The book has been praised for being a profoundly important work. The few criticisms of the book state that the stories run together and are often repetitive and the author’s presentation of the subject is completely one-sided, not taking into account the social problems of indigenous or traditional societies. If you were to rate this book, how many stars out of five would you give it, and why?
